svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks. A lifecycle hook provides a specified amount of time, one hour by default, to wait for the action to complete before the instance transitions to the next state. On scale out the hook puts the instance into a wait state called Pending:Wait and performs a custom action; if more time is needed the timeout period can be restarted by recording a heartbeat. What happens when the timeout elapses is set by the hook's DefaultResult, documented as the action the Auto Scaling group takes when the lifecycle hook timeout elapses or if an unexpected failure occurs, with valid values CONTINUE and ABANDON and a default value of ABANDON, so for a launch hook ABANDON causes the instance to be terminated and replaced while CONTINUE allows the launch process to proceed. The heartbeat timeout has a range from 30 to 7200 seconds and a default of 3600 seconds. The instance then enters the InService state and the health check grace period starts, which is exactly why a launch hook is the documented alternative to a long health check grace period: the hook does its waiting before InService, so the grace period does not have to cover bootstrap time. On scale in the hook puts the instance into Terminating:Wait, and after the action completes or the timeout expires the instance transitions to Terminating:Proceed and is terminated. The result of a lifecycle hook can be either abandon or continue, and the meaning differs by direction. If an instance is launching, continue indicates the actions were successful and Auto Scaling can put the instance into service, while abandon indicates the custom actions were unsuccessful and the instance can be terminated and replaced. If an instance is terminating, both abandon and continue allow the instance to terminate; abandon stops any remaining actions such as other lifecycle hooks, while continue allows any other lifecycle hooks to complete. That is the trap: a termination hook does not block termination. By default, termination lifecycle hooks operate on a best-effort basis, and if a termination lifecycle hook times out or is abandoned, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling proceeds with terminating the instance immediately. Retention requires a separate instance lifecycle policy: without one the instance proceeds to termination immediately even if the termination lifecycle action completed with an ABANDON result, whereas with a policy configured to retain instances on TerminateHookAbandon the instance moves to a retained state. Retained instances continue to incur standard EC2 charges, do not count toward the group's desired capacity so replacements are launched, and are ignored by instance refresh and max instance lifetime. Timeouts are bounded: the default heartbeat timeout is one hour and there is also a global timeout that is 48 hours or 100 times the heartbeat timeout, whichever is smaller, so with the default heartbeat the ceiling is 48 hours, which is two days. Other limits: a lifecycle hook does not prevent a Spot Instance from terminating when capacity is no longer available, which can happen at any time with a two-minute interruption notice; Auto Scaling limits the rate at which it allows instances to launch if the lifecycle hooks are failing consistently; hooks do not apply when you attach or detach instances, move instances in and out of standby mode, or delete the group with the force delete option; multiple hooks added at group creation must share the same notification target and IAM role; and scaling activities from simple scaling policies are paused until the lifecycle actions have completed and the cooldown period has expired.
svg.title: Abandon and continue both terminate the instance; only a policy retains it
svg.text: A termination hook does not stop a termination. Neither result does.
“If an instance is terminating, both abandon and continue allow the instance to terminate. However,
abandon stops any remaining actions, such as other lifecycle hooks…”
Launch: the wait happens before InService, which is the whole point
Pending → Pending:Wait → complete(CONTINUE) → Pending:Proceed → register with LB → InService
“The instance enters the InService state and the health check grace period starts.”
So the hook covers bootstrap, and the grace period no longer has to. On timeout, DefaultResult decides.
Terminate: the wait happens, then the instance dies either way
deregister from LB → Terminating:Wait → (complete or 1h timeout) → Terminating:Proceed → gone
abandon stops later hooks. continue lets them run. Both end in termination.
Best-effort by default, which is not what most people assume they bought
“By default, termination lifecycle hooks operate on a best-effort basis. If a termination lifecycle hook
times out, or is abandoned, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling proceeds with terminating the instance immediately.”
A hook written to flush state does not guarantee the state is flushed. It guarantees you were asked.
RETENTION IS A SEPARATE FEATURE
instance lifecycle policy
retain on TerminateHookAbandon
Without it, ABANDON still terminates. With it,
the instance moves to a retained state.
WHAT A RETAINED INSTANCE COSTS
Keeps incurring standard EC2 charges
Does not count toward desired capacity,
so a replacement launches alongside it
Ignored by instance refresh and max lifetime
The two clocks
heartbeat 3600s default, range 30-7200 · restart it by recording a heartbeat
global “48 hours or 100 times the heartbeat timeout, whichever is smaller” → 48h
A hook does not save a Spot Instance: it “does not prevent an instance from terminating in the event that capacity is no
longer available”, on a two-minute notice.
And consistently failing hooks are throttled: AWS limits the launch rate rather than letting a broken hook churn.
